place.zh: 沂中医 · 城里的医院 · 十一月底
place.en: Yizhong · the hospital in town · late November

setup.zh: 「凑数的。」他背着人「闭关三日」，晨脉八十八，回了一个「好」，蹲完了。夜里尿成可乐色：横纹肌溶解。出院那天，阿禾的纸上三条。
setup.en: "Just making up the numbers." He trains three days in secret; morning pulse 88; he answers "OK" and finishes the squats anyway. That night his urine is cola: rhabdomyolysis. On discharge, three lines on Ahe's paper.

recap.zh: 练太猛，横纹肌溶解，住院三天；「数是你自己报的」——晨脉七十以下，才许摸球。
recap.en: Overtrained, rhabdomyolysis, three days in hospital; "you report the numbers yourself" — under seventy in the morning, then the ball.

zh: 晨脉回到七十以下，才许摸球。
en: Under seventy in the morning — then the ball.

story.zh:
十一月二十一日，小组赛第三轮。针推的替补席上照例摆着一排纸杯，杯口朝下，杯底拿记号笔写着号——阿禾的规矩：谁上过场，下来喝水，就把自己那只翻过来。沈芒拄着拐坐在看台上，数了两遍：十一只。

他那只「0」，没摆上去。

散场时，马小宝穿着中药学院胸前印「33」的新球衣晃过来，拿摇杯点了点他的拐：「零号。一队报十二个人，少一个报不上名——你就是来凑数的。」古籍部那一夜，两个人谁也没再提过。

这话一个字也没说错，所以格外疼。可疼完了，他心里又有一样东西悄悄松了一下：凑数的，没人看，不用站上那条罚球线。这一松，他自己也吓了一跳，赶紧按了回去。

那天夜里，老蔡的手机从上铺垂下来，屏幕停在一行字上：「……少年闭关三日，出关之时，连破两境。」

半决赛在二十八号。他在备忘录里写下「闭关三日」：四点四十起，五点到球馆，背一书包书深蹲，靠墙静蹲到蹲不住；脚踝不跳。末一行加了粗：不许告诉阿禾。

头一天，静蹲三分十秒，他拿粉笔写在看台底下那块蓝软包上。第二天腿硬得像两根晾了一夜的油条，他想起在哪儿看过一句：疼，就是在长。当天深蹲加到了七百个。静蹲：两分零五。

第三天四点四十，他躺着量晨脉，照规矩发给阿禾：八十八。平日七十上下。五点十分，他蹲到第二百个，手机一震：

「88？今天别练。」

他回了一个字：「好。」揣回兜里，蹲完了剩下的。静蹲，一分二十。软包上三行粉笔字，一行比一行短，像三级往下走的台阶。

于是就有了那天夜里十一点的那一泡。他在厕所里站了一分钟，到底没忍住，出来对两位室友道：「我的尿，是可乐色的。」

眼镜已经在搜了，脸色一点一点变了：「我查了。腿疼得碰不得、没劲、尿是可乐色——横纹肌溶解。肉崩了，漏进血里，伤肾。马上去医院。」老蔡从上铺探出半个身子，一脸肃穆：「走火入魔。」

眼镜一面穿鞋，一面给阿禾打了电话。沈芒扑过去夺手机，腿一软，没夺着。

凌晨一点，急诊。大夫念化验单：「肌酸激酶，四万二。」沈芒问高吗，大夫道：「正常人一两百。」

走廊尽头的门开了。进来的是阿禾，长羽绒服底下露着一截睡裤，白球鞋没穿袜子，马尾扎歪了。她走到推床跟前，先看那袋盐水，又看那张单子，看了很久，掏出本子写了一行，合上。合上以前，沈芒瞥见十一月二十四日那一行，只一个字：「腿。」

她一个字也没说。他宁可她骂他。

住院三天。护士每天早上拎起尿壶对着窗户照：「可乐。」「乌龙茶。」「大麦茶。」沈芒每听一声，便往被子里缩一截，缩到第三天，只剩一撮头发露在外头。隔壁床的魏大叔五十来岁，也是这个病：年会要穿十年前的西装，扣子扣不上，报了个动感单车班，一天三节，上了三天。他叹气：「人到了哪个岁数，都觉得自己三天能成。」

眼镜来了，摸出那本卷了边的《抱朴子内篇》：「葛洪那会儿没『走火入魔』这个词，倒有一句比它准：『力所不胜，而强举之，伤也。』」沈芒道：「我举得动啊。七百个呢。」眼镜拿指头点着那个「强」字：「你举得动的是那一下。伤不是哪一下伤的，是一天一天攒的。」

下午阿禾来了，在床尾坐下，点着本子上那个八十八：「练完是挖坑。吃饱睡足，坑填平了，还多出一截——长的是那一截。晨脉高一截，就是坑还没填平。你一个坑没填，又往下挖了两天。」

夜里十点，妈的视频准时打过来。他举高手机：「宿舍呢。」妈听了一会儿：「你那屋里，嘀、嘀、嘀的，是啥？」——隔壁床的输液泵。她在县城超市收了十来年银，扫码枪哪一声不对，隔两个收银台都听得出。「芒，你把手机转过去。」镜头扫过白墙、床栏，停在那袋盐水上。一滴，一滴。「滴得挺匀。」她说。爸的脸挤进来，皱着眉看了半天：「我跑了二十年长途。开四个钟头，必须歇二十分钟。不歇的，我见过，都在沟里。」

二十八日晚上，半决赛，他在病床上看手机直播。针推赢了药学四分。镜头扫过替补席，纸杯摆了十二只——他那只「0」也摆上了，扣着。散场以后，马小宝发来一张记分牌的照片：「凑数的，决赛见。躺着可不算数。」

二十九日出院，阿禾在医院门口递给他一张纸，三条：晨脉回到七十以下，才许摸球；摸了球，只许罚球；十二月六号复查抽血。

两个人站着等车，谁也没说话。沈芒憋不住了：「阿禾，你还生气呢？」

阿禾看着马路对面：「你练，我不气。练坏了，我也不气，谁都有头一回。」她停了一停，「我气的是，那天早上我问了你，你说好。」

他张了张嘴，什么也没说出来。十月里两回，他说吃的是食堂。

「你的数，我天天记。」阿禾道，「数是你自己报的。你报了实话，又不听，那我这本子，记的是什么？」

车来了。她先上了车，没回头。
story.en:
November 21st, round three of the group stage. On Acupuncture and Tuina's bench, as usual, stood a row of paper cups, mouths down, numbers written on their bottoms in marker — Ahe's rule: whoever had played came off for a drink and turned his own cup over. Shen Mang sat in the stands on his crutches and counted twice: eleven.

His cup, "0," hadn't been set out.

When the game broke up, Ma Xiaobao sauntered over in the College of Chinese Materia Medica's new jersey with "33" on the chest, and tapped Shen Mang's crutch with his shaker bottle: "Number Zero. A team registers twelve, and one short means they can't enter — you're just here to make up the numbers." Neither of them had mentioned that night in the Rare Books Room since.

Not one word of it was wrong, which was why it hurt so much. But once the hurt passed, something in him quietly loosened: a number-filler, nobody watching, no need to step up to that free-throw line. The loosening startled him, and he hurried to push it back down.

That night, Old Cai's phone dangled down from the top bunk, its screen stopped on a line: "...The youth went into secluded cultivation for three days, and when he came out of seclusion he broke through two realms in a row."

The semifinal was on the 28th. In his notes he wrote "Three days of secluded cultivation": up at four forty, at the gym by five, squats with a backpack full of books, wall sits until he couldn't hold them; no jumping, for the ankle. The last line, in bold: Don't tell Ahe.

On the first day his wall sit was three minutes ten, and he chalked it on the blue padding under the stands. On the second day his legs were as stiff as two fried dough sticks left out overnight, and he remembered a line he'd read somewhere: pain means you're growing. That day he took his squats up to seven hundred. Wall sit: two minutes five.

On the third day, at four forty, he took his morning pulse lying down and, as the rule said, sent it to Ahe: eighty-eight. Usually it was around seventy. At five ten, on his two hundredth squat, his phone buzzed:

"88? No training today."

He replied with one word: "OK." He pocketed the phone and finished the rest of the squats. Wall sit: one minute twenty. Three lines of chalk on the padding, each shorter than the last, like three steps going down.

And that was how he came to that eleven o'clock pee. He stood in the bathroom for a minute, and in the end he couldn't keep it to himself; he came out and said to his two roommates, "My pee is cola-colored."

Specs was already searching, and his face changed bit by bit: "I looked it up. Legs too sore to touch, no strength, cola-colored urine — rhabdomyolysis. The muscle breaks down, leaks into the blood, damages the kidneys. Hospital, now." Old Cai leaned half out of the top bunk, his face solemn: "Qi deviation."

Specs called Ahe while he put on his shoes. Shen Mang lunged for the phone, his legs gave way, and he missed.

One in the morning, the ER. The doctor read out the lab sheet: "Creatine kinase, forty-two thousand." Shen Mang asked if that was high. The doctor said, "A normal person's is one or two hundred."

The door at the end of the corridor opened. In came Ahe, pajama bottoms showing under her long down coat, white sneakers with no socks, her ponytail crooked. She walked up to the gurney, looked first at the bag of saline, then at the lab sheet, for a long time, then took out her notebook, wrote a line, and closed it. Before it shut, Shen Mang caught the entry for November 24th, just one word: "Legs."

She didn't say a single word. He'd rather she had yelled at him.

Three days in the hospital. Every morning the nurse held the urinal up to the window: "Cola." "Oolong." "Barley tea." With every word Shen Mang shrank a little further under the blanket, until by the third day only a tuft of hair showed. In the next bed was Uncle Wei, fiftyish, with the same thing: he had to wear a ten-year-old suit to his company's year-end party and couldn't button it, so he signed up for spin classes, three a day, for three days. He sighed: "No matter what age you get to, you always think you can do it in three days."

Specs came and fished out his dog-eared copy of the Baopuzi, Inner Chapters: "Ge Hong didn't have the words 'qi deviation' back then, but he had a line that's more precise: 'When strength cannot bear it and one forces the lift, that is injury.'" Shen Mang said, "But I could lift it. Seven hundred of them." Specs tapped his finger on the word "forces": "What you could lift was each single one. Injury doesn't come from any single one. It piles up, day by day."

In the afternoon, Ahe came and sat at the foot of the bed, tapping the eighty-eight in her notebook: "Training digs a hole. Eat well, sleep enough, and the hole fills back up, with a bit extra on top — that extra bit is what grows. When your morning pulse is up, the hole isn't filled yet. You didn't fill one hole, and then you dug down for two more days."

At ten that night, Mom's video call came in right on time. He held the phone up high: "In the dorm." Mom listened for a moment: "What's that beep, beep, beep in your room?" — the infusion pump at the next bed. She had worked the register at a county-town supermarket for over ten years; if a scanner beeped wrong, she could hear it two checkouts away. "Mang, turn the phone around." The camera swept over a white wall, a bed rail, and stopped on the bag of saline. Drip. Drip. "Dripping nice and even," she said. Dad's face squeezed into the frame and frowned at it for a long time: "I drove long-haul for twenty years. Four hours behind the wheel, you have to rest twenty minutes. The ones who didn't rest — I've seen them. All in the ditch."

On the night of the 28th, the semifinal, he watched the livestream on his phone from his hospital bed. Acupuncture and Tuina beat Pharmacy by four. The camera swept over the bench: twelve paper cups — his "0" had been set out too, mouth down. After the game, Ma Xiaobao sent a photo of the scoreboard: "Number-filler, see you in the final. Lying down doesn't count."

He was discharged on the 29th. At the hospital entrance, Ahe handed him a sheet of paper with three rules: morning pulse back under seventy before he could touch a ball; once he touched a ball, free throws only; recheck bloodwork on December 6th.

The two of them stood waiting for the bus, and neither said anything. Shen Mang couldn't hold it in: "Ahe, are you still angry?"

Ahe looked across the road: "You training doesn't make me angry. You training yourself into the ground doesn't make me angry either — everyone has a first time." She paused. "What makes me angry is that I asked you that morning, and you said OK."

He opened his mouth, and nothing came out. Twice in October, he'd said he had eaten at the cafeteria.

"I write your numbers down every day," said Ahe. "The numbers are what you report yourself. If you report the truth and then don't listen, then what is this notebook of mine keeping track of?"

The bus came. She got on first, and didn't look back.

exits.means: waits for the morning pulse to come down before touching the ball

refuse.zh: 晨脉还没回到七十以下。
refuse.en: The morning pulse isn't under seventy yet.

story.zh:
七十六，七十二。什么也不许干，只许吃、睡、躺着，他头一回知道歇着也要咬牙。十二月二日早上六点，他两根指头搭在腕子上数了两遍：六十九。他一骨碌坐起来，脑袋「咚」地撞在上铺床板上。老蔡迷迷糊糊地问几点了，他捂着脑袋，眼泪都撞出来了，咧着嘴道：「出关了。」

阿禾回了一个字：「记。」

十二月七日，露天球场，北风刮得篮网横着飘，他十投二。夜里，学校表白墙出了一条决赛竞猜，两支队二十四个名字，各跟着一个百分数。他的手指一直划到最末一行：

「0号　沈芒（针推）　上场概率：1%」

底下点赞最多的评论：「那1%，是怕他哭。」

他盯着那个「1%」看了很久。看着看着，倒觉得这个数挺好：一百回里头有一回，就是说，还有一回。
story.en:
Seventy-six, seventy-two. He wasn't allowed to do anything but eat, sleep, and lie around, and for the first time he learned that resting takes gritted teeth too. At six in the morning on December 2nd, he laid two fingers on his wrist and counted twice: sixty-nine. He sat bolt upright, and his head went thunk against the boards of the top bunk. Old Cai asked groggily what time it was; clutching his head, tears knocked into his eyes, Shen Mang grinned: "Out of seclusion."

Ahe replied with one word: "Noted."

December 7th, the outdoor court, the north wind blowing the net sideways; he went two for ten. That night, the school's confessions wall put up a poll for the final: twenty-four names from the two teams, each followed by a percentage. His finger scrolled all the way down to the last line:

"No. 0  Shen Mang (Acu-Tuina)  Chance of playing: 1%"

The most-liked comment below: "That 1% is so he won't cry."

He stared at that "1%" for a long time. The longer he stared, the more he liked the number: one time in a hundred meant there was still one time.
